question: This food-preference meme often pairs its central character’s favorite snack with her aversion to carrots, creating a contrast between two foods. The child at the center of the joke can read minds, which lets her discover secrets that her adoptive parents hide. Her father Loid is a spy and her mother Yor is an assassin, although the household presents itself as an ordinary family. Fans of Spy x Family turn this young Forger’s enthusiasm for a particular crunchy legume into captions and other jokes. For 10 points, give this short meme declaration naming the telepathic girl and the food she especially enjoys as a snack.

The initial official English release of a panel associated with this meme used a single negative word before a correction restored its familiar wording. That panel appears in chapter 221 of Gege Akutami’s manga and echoes an earlier exchange from the third chapter. Edits replace the pictured character or redraw the panel, often making the speaker’s confidence look increasingly implausible or comically misplaced. Satoru Gojo delivers the reply in Jujutsu Kaisen when discussing a possible confrontation with Sukuna and dismissing the prospect of defeat. For 10 points, give this confident response predicting victory, beginning with a casual alternative to the word “no”.

The speaker of this declaration apologizes to Riko Amanai while acknowledging that his current euphoric feeling has displaced his grief. He has recovered from a seemingly fatal encounter by learning to use a reverse cursed technique to heal himself. During his rematch with Toji Fushiguro, this sorcerer floats above his opponent before demonstrating an attack called Hollow Purple. The line spoken by Satoru Gojo echoes a saying associated with the Buddha and expresses an overwhelming sense of personal supremacy. For 10 points, give this Jujutsu Kaisen declaration in which Gojo claims a uniquely exalted status across both celestial and terrestrial realms.
answer: “Throughout heaven and earth, I alone am the honored one” [or “I alone am the honored one”; or “I alone am the honoured one”; or “Throughout heaven and earth I alone am the honoured one”; or “The honored one”; or “The honoured one”; or “I am the honored one”; or “I am the honoured one”]

question: The recipient of this compliment imagines his companions Hanami and Dagon near the end of a battle he cannot survive. That recipient had helped awaken his eventual opponent by feeding cursed fingers to Yuji, hoping to recruit the being within him. Hearing his abilities acknowledged causes the defeated cursed spirit to shed tears, despite previously being treated dismissively by Satoru Gojo. Sukuna delivers this rare praise to Jogo, a volcano-headed opponent whose attacks include fiery techniques and a massive meteor. For 10 points, give this Jujutsu Kaisen line that encourages the defeated fighter to retain his dignity and recognizes his formidable ability.
answer: “Stand proud, you’re strong” [or “Stand proud you are strong”; or “Stand proud”]

question: An official promotional upload repeated the sequence associated with this chant for a full hour before the corresponding television anime premiered. Posted in May 2024, that loop shows Torako dancing while facing a deer, creating an unusually persistent musical advertisement. Fans recreated the movement with other characters, turning the repeated snippet into a dance meme well beyond the original promotional video. The syllables form the Japanese title of the series known in English as My Deer Friend Nokotan and appear in its opening music. For 10 points, identify this deer-themed dance meme by its repeated Japanese chant or the title of the opening song that supplies it.
answer: “Shikanoko nokonoko koshitantan” [or “Shikanoko nokonoko koshi tantan”; or “Shikanokonokonokokoshitantan”; or “Shikairo Days”; or “Shikairo Days Dance”; or “Shikanoko”]

question: The character associated with this greeting is designated laboratory member number 002 and spends some of her spare time making cosplay outfits. She is a childhood friend of Rintaro Okabe, whose attempts to alter events place her at the center of repeated crises. Using the nickname Mayushii for herself, she delivers the sound in a cheerful, singsong manner when introducing herself or arriving. This greeting belongs to Mayuri Shiina in Steins;Gate, providing a lighthearted contrast to the series’ increasingly dangerous experiments with time. For 10 points, imitate or name this brief melodic greeting, usually romanized with an opening “tu” and an extended final vowel.

The character who uses this expression gives himself the theatrical alias Hououin Kyouma, presenting his activities as those of a mad scientist. He claims to face a mysterious Organization, mixing grandiose conspiratorial language with the everyday life of his small laboratory. His Reading Steiner ability lets him remember events after changes to the timeline, making him crucial to the story’s time-travel experiments. Rintaro Okabe repeatedly utters this peculiar three-word catchphrase in Steins;Gate, even though the expression itself has no established meaning. For 10 points, give this cryptic phrase associated with Okabe, whose final word is often romanized with either an initial K or C.

An early documented appearance of this meme was on the Tanasinn wiki in 2007, alongside a screenshot featuring Light Yagami. A translator’s note at the top of the image explains a Japanese term that the subtitle has unnecessarily left untranslated. The caption became a way to mock fan translations that preserve Japanese vocabulary even when a straightforward English equivalent exists. Its final word refers to an intended course of action, so the explanatory annotation undermines the apparent need to retain that foreign term in the first place. For 10 points, give this Death Note subtitle meme expressing that events have unfolded as intended, in its mixed-language wording or its English equivalent.
answer: “Just according to keikaku” [or “All according to keikaku”; or “Keikaku”; or “Just as planned”; or “Just according to plan”; or “All according to plan”]

question: This line’s visual presentation includes slow motion and sparkling fragments, giving an everyday action an extravagantly dramatic treatment on screen. YouTube Poop remixes of the scene appeared in 2007, helping turn its delivery into a recurring joke among online viewers. The original scene appears in “Glare”, the eighth episode of an anime about a notebook that can cause a person’s death. Light Yagami delivers this declaration in Death Note, announcing an ordinary snack-related action with the intensity of a decisive strategic maneuver. For 10 points, give this melodramatic line in which Kira declares his intention to consume a single thin, crispy fried slice.
answer: “I’ll take a potato chip and eat it” [or “I will take a potato chip and eat it”; or “Potato chip”]

question: Edits of this viral boast have included Monika from Doki Doki Literature Club, placing an unrelated fictional character into the joke. Other remixes inserted the clip into scenes from Revenge of the Sith, recasting its speaker as an unexpectedly confident combatant. The original live-action video spread through Twitter and YouTube in July 2017 and ends with the child’s emphatic battle cry. The speaker announces two very different sources of support before shouting, combining religious backing with enthusiasm for Japanese animated entertainment. For 10 points, name this meme boast claiming that both a divine being and a favorite animation medium are supporting the speaker.
answer: “The power of God and anime” [or “I have the power of God and anime on my side”; or “God and anime”]

question: Context for this notorious subtitle involves Avalon, an implanted magical sheath responsible for its speaker’s unusually effective ability to recover from injuries. Kiritsugu Emiya placed that object inside the speaker, explaining why a seemingly obvious observation about mortality had a less ordinary context. Removed from that context, the sentence circulated alongside reaction jokes expressing disbelief that such an obvious statement needed to be spoken. Shirou Emiya delivers the line in Studio Deen’s 2006 adaptation of Fate/stay night, where supernatural survival complicates ordinary expectations. For 10 points, give this tautological anime quote asserting that a fatal attack normally results in the victim’s death.
answer: “People die if they are killed” [or “People die when they are killed”]

question: This nickname praises a television adaptation directed by Takahiro Miura, whose first season aired in 2014 and whose second followed in 2015. The production adapts a route from a Type-Moon visual novel, following Shirou Emiya’s involvement in the fifth Holy Grail War. Fans use the phrase to praise ufotable’s lavish animation, especially the visual spectacle accompanying battles between mages and summoned heroes. The joke alters the subtitle of this Fate/stay night adaptation by substituting a term for financial resources for a word describing weapons. For 10 points, give this three-word anime nickname suggesting that the studio had no spending ceiling when producing its impressive action scenes.

A line spoken by Quentin Quire in an X-Men comic has been interpreted as a reference to this familiar anime meme. The command is associated with a character whose clasped hands and stern expression have inspired their own widely imitated pose. That character, Gendo Ikari, leads NERV and maintains a troubled relationship with the teenage son whom he summons to pilot Unit 01. Fans of Neon Genesis Evangelion use this impatient order as a shorthand for a father’s demand that his reluctant child become a pilot. For 10 points, give this meme instruction telling the younger Ikari to enter the giant machine he is expected to control.
answer: “Get in the robot, Shinji” [or “Get in the robot”]

question: The episode ending with this repeated word carries the alternate English title “Take Care of Yourself” and focuses on Instrumentality. Earlier in that episode, an alternate reality presents familiar characters as ordinary students and family members in a domestic-comedy setting. Shinji comes to recognize that he can change how he understands himself, culminating in a scene surrounded by familiar faces. The cast applauds him while repeating this expression at the end of the original Neon Genesis Evangelion television series. For 10 points, give this celebratory word, or its Japanese equivalent, that the characters address to Shinji during the famous finale.

This Japanese command appears beneath a red-tinted bird in a reaction image used to express disapproval or disagreement. Despite that image’s common name, the photographed bird is a grackle, and its captioned version circulated on Imgur in 2017. Grammatically, this expression uses the plain imperative form of a verb meaning to cease an activity or to quit. The final syllable of this conjugated command is “ro”, giving learners a way to distinguish it from softer requests. For 10 points, give this forceful Japanese command meaning “stop it”, or name the disapproving bird meme that uses it as a caption.
answer: “Yamero” [or “Crow of Judgement”; or “Crow of Judgment”; or “Yamero Crow”]

question: Flash animations drew on a 1998 Capcom fighting game to spread this shouted phrase, often combining it with exaggerated attack sequences. The associated visual effect changes the surrounding colors before movement freezes, allowing the attacker to act while opponents remain motionless. Knives and a steamroller feature among attacks linked with the character who shouts this phrase during his confrontation with Jotaro. Dio uses it to invoke his time-stopping Stand in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, and fans reproduce the Japanese pronunciation for comic emphasis. For 10 points, give this shouted Stand name, whose English translation names the entire planet and whose pronunciation became an internet catchphrase.

The music associated with this video meme comes from a Yes recording included on the progressive-rock band’s 1971 album Fragile. The tune served as an ending theme during the anime adaptations of Phantom Blood and Battle Tendency, linking it with cliffhangers. Online edits spread through Vine and YouTube, timing the musical buildup to an ordinary scene about to go spectacularly wrong. A freeze-frame and a prominent arrow interrupt the action before its outcome, imitating an ending device from JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. For 10 points, name this cliffhanger meme by its arrow’s three-word caption, or identify the Yes song used to build suspense before the freeze-frame.

This reveal comes from an early Phantom Blood encounter and appears in the first episode of the 2012 television adaptation. Its speaker targets Erina Pendleton in an attempt to humiliate Jonathan Joestar, turning a romantic expectation into an unwanted surprise. The scene follows a stolen kiss, after which the antagonist triumphantly identifies himself as the person responsible for the encounter. Online variations use the declaration as a bait-and-switch punchline, replacing something expected with the grinning villain from JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. For 10 points, give this villain’s Japanese self-reveal, or its familiar English rendering, announcing that he was the unexpected culprit.
answer: “Kono Dio da” [or “It was me Dio”; or “But it was me Dio”]

question: Professional wrestler Marcellus Black adopted this catchphrase in connection with a running-knee attack, taking an idol joke into another performance setting. The original anime scene appears in a fifth episode from 2013, when a character demonstrates how a proper idol should behave. Fans remixed the repeated syllables into videos and musical edits, often preserving the speaker’s exaggeratedly cheerful delivery and hand gestures. The performer is Yazawa, a school idol from the Love Live franchise who uses the routine as her distinctive introduction. For 10 points, give this singsong idol catchphrase, built around a repeated two-syllable name and usually accompanied by a deliberately adorable pose.
answer: “Nico Nico Nii” [or “Nico Nico Ni”; or “NicoNicoNii”; or “Niko Niko Nii”]
